intro: Everything in this topic comes from one relation: **distance = speed x time**. The questions differ only in which of the three is the same for both parts of the story.

There are eight short lessons, about people and vehicles on the move. Go in order the first time. **Trains** now have a topic of their own, which adds one idea (a train has length); it is the natural one to do straight after this.
after: That is the whole topic. The **Quick revision** tab has the km/h to m/s table and every question type on one page, and the Course in each bank has many more.
When a question looks tangled, come back to two plain checks: are my units the same, and what exactly is the distance being covered?

lessons.title: Distance, speed and time
lessons.plain: The starting point: one small relation, and the habit of keeping the units the same.
teach: **Speed** tells you how much distance is covered in each unit of time. 60 km/h means 60 kilometres in every hour. From that one sentence you get the only relation this topic needs:
**distance = speed x time**
Know any two and you have the third: speed = distance / time, and time = distance / speed.
Nearly every slip in the early questions is a **units** slip. Before you multiply or divide, make sure the units agree.
- If the speed is in km/h, the time must be in hours and the distance in km.
- If the speed is in m/s (metres per second), the time must be in seconds and the distance in metres.
To change between the two kinds of speed:
- **km/h to m/s: multiply by 5/18.** 72 km/h is 72 x 5/18 = 20 m/s.
- **m/s to km/h: multiply by 18/5.** 10 m/s is 36 km/h.
Where does 5/18 come from? One kilometre is 1,000 metres and one hour is 3,600 seconds, and 1,000 / 3,600 = 5/18. A handy anchor: **18 km/h is 5 m/s**, so 36 is 10, 54 is 15, 72 is 20 and 90 is 25.
For minutes, remember that 30 minutes is half an hour and 50 minutes is 50/60 = 5/6 of an hour.

example.q: A bus is moving at 54 km/h. How many metres does it cover in 20 seconds?
steps: The time is in seconds and the answer is wanted in metres, so change the speed to m/s.
Distance = speed x time = 15 x 20 = 300 metres.

check.q: A man walks 900 metres in 10 minutes. What is his speed in km/h?
check.why: 10 minutes is 600 seconds, so his speed is 900 / 600 = 1.5 m/s. In km/h: 1.5 x 18/5 = 5.4. (1.5 is the speed in m/s.)

lessons.title: The same distance at two speeds
lessons.plain: New: two people, or one person on two days, cover the same distance. Faster means less time, in the opposite ratio.
teach: When the **distance is the same**, speed and time pull in opposite directions. Go twice as fast and you need half the time.
So if two speeds are in the ratio 3 : 4, the times for the same distance are in the ratio **4 : 3**. Just turn the ratio round.
This turns a whole family of questions into ratio questions. They never tell you the distance; they tell you a **gap in time**.
"The speeds of A and B are in the ratio 2 : 3. A takes 15 minutes more than B for the same distance."
- Times are 3 : 2.
- The gap in time is 3 - 2 = 1 part, and it is 15 minutes.
- So A takes 45 minutes and B takes 30.

The same idea covers one person changing speed. "Walking at three-fourths of his usual speed, a man is 20 minutes late." His speed is 3/4 of usual, so his time is **4/3** of usual. The extra one-third of his usual time is the 20 minutes, so his usual time is 60 minutes.
Words such as "twice as fast" are a speed ratio in disguise: 2 : 1. A chain of them ("A is twice as fast as B, and B is thrice as fast as C") is built up from the slowest: C is 1, B is 3, A is 6.

example.q: The speeds of A and B are in the ratio 2 : 3. To cover the same distance, A takes 15 minutes more than B. How long does B take?
steps: Same distance, so turn the speed ratio round: times are 3 : 2.
The gap in time is 3 - 2 = 1 part = 15 minutes.
B has 2 parts: 30 minutes.

check.q: Walking at four-fifths of his usual speed, a man reaches his office 10 minutes late. What is his usual time?
check.why: Speed is 4/5 of usual, so time is 5/4 of usual. The extra quarter is 10 minutes, so the usual time is 40 minutes. (50 is today's time.)

shortcut.title: A change in speed as a fraction
text: If the speed goes up by **1/n**, the time comes down by **1/(n + 1)**. If the speed comes down by 1/n, the time goes up by 1/(n - 1). It is the turn-around from Percentages once more.
Speed up by 1/4 (25% faster): time is 1/5 less. Speed down by 1/4: time is 1/3 more.
So "at three-fourths of his speed he is 20 minutes late": the speed is down by 1/4, the time is up by 1/3, and 1/3 of the usual time is 20 minutes.

lessons.title: Late, early, and changing the speed
lessons.plain: New: the gap in time comes from being late one day and early another, or the speed must change to save time.
teach: "At 40 km/h he reaches office 10 minutes late. At 50 km/h he reaches 5 minutes early." This is last lesson's question with the gap in time hidden.
Late on one day and early on the other: the two journeys differ by 10 + 5 = **15 minutes**. (If he were late on both days, by 10 and by 4 minutes, the gap would be the difference, 6 minutes.)
Now proceed as before.
- Speeds 40 : 50 = 4 : 5, so times are 5 : 4.
- The gap is 1 part = 15 minutes.
- At 40 km/h he takes 5 parts = 75 minutes, which is 1.25 hours.
- Distance = 40 x 1.25 = 50 km.

**Changing the speed to save time.** "A car covers 450 km in 9 hours. By how much must its speed rise to do it in 7.5 hours?" Find both speeds and subtract. Present speed 50, needed speed 60: a rise of 10 km/h. Read whether the question wants the **new speed** or the **increase**.
If the time is to be cut by a fraction, think of what is **left**. Cutting the time by three-fifths leaves two-fifths of it, so the speed must become 5/2 of what it was, which is 150% more.

**When only a difference in speed and a difference in time are given**, such as "10 km/h faster would save 1 hour over 200 km", the proper method is a heavier equation. Test the options instead: try a speed, work out both times, and see whether they differ by an hour.

example.q: Travelling at 30 km/h a man reaches his office 10 minutes late. Travelling at 40 km/h he reaches 5 minutes early. Find the distance to his office.
steps: Late one day, early the other: the journeys differ by 10 + 5 = 15 minutes.
Speeds 30 : 40 = 3 : 4, so times are 4 : 3.
The gap is 1 part = 15 minutes.
At 30 km/h he takes 4 parts = 60 minutes = 1 hour.
Distance = 30 x 1 = 30 km.

check.q: A car covers a certain distance in 6 hours at 50 km/h. At what speed must it travel to cover the same distance in 5 hours?
check.why: Distance = 50 x 6 = 300 km. In 5 hours: 300 / 5 = 60 km/h.

shortcut.title: Late and early in one line
text: For two speeds **a** and **b** over the same distance, with a time gap **t** between the journeys:
Use hours for t. With 40 km/h and 50 km/h and a gap of 15 minutes (1/4 hour): (40 x 50 x 1/4) / 10 = 50 km.
It is the ratio method with the steps folded together. If you forget it, the ratio method is always there.

lessons.title: Average speed
lessons.plain: New: a journey at two or more speeds. The average speed is total distance over total time, never the average of the speeds.
teach: "A man goes from A to B at 40 km/h and returns at 60 km/h. What is his average speed?" The tempting answer is 50. It is wrong, and seeing why is the lesson.
He spends **more time** on the slow leg than on the fast one, so the slow speed counts for more. The honest definition is:
**average speed = total distance / total time**
When the distance is not given, **choose one that suits you**. Pick a number both speeds go into: 120 km each way.
- Going: 120 / 40 = 3 hours. Returning: 120 / 60 = 2 hours.
- Total distance 240 km, total time 5 hours.
- Average speed = 240 / 5 = 48 km/h.
Any distance you choose gives 48. It is a little below 50, as it should be.
First check **what is equal** in the question.
- **Equal distances** (there and back, or "one-third of the way at each speed"): choose a convenient distance, as above.
- **Times are given** ("5 km/h for 2 hours, then 15 km/h for 3 hours"): simply add up the distances and divide by the total time.
Average speed also works backwards. If the average speed for a return trip is 48 km/h and the trip takes 5 hours, the total distance is 240 km, so one way is 120 km.

example.q: A man goes to a town at 30 km/h and comes back at 20 km/h. What is his average speed for the whole journey?
steps: Equal distances, so choose one that both speeds go into: 60 km each way.
Going: 60 / 30 = 2 hours. Returning: 60 / 20 = 3 hours.
Total distance 120 km, total time 5 hours.
Average speed = 120 / 5 = 24 km/h.

check.q: A car travels at 30 km/h for 2 hours and then at 60 km/h for 1 hour. What is its average speed?
check.why: Here the times are given, so add the distances: 60 + 60 = 120 km in 3 hours. 120 / 3 = 40 km/h. (45 is the plain average of the speeds.)

shortcut.title: Two equal distances
text: For two **equal distances** at speeds **a** and **b**, the average speed is:
Use it only when the two distances are equal. If the two **times** are equal instead, the average speed really is the plain average of the two speeds.

lessons.title: A journey in parts
lessons.plain: New: the journey is split into stretches, and the question asks about one stretch, the total time, or the speed still needed.
teach: Longer journey questions break the trip into stretches. The method is bookkeeping: **for each stretch, write its distance, its speed and its time.** Two of the three are usually given, and the third is one division away. Then add up what the question asks for.
A small table keeps it tidy.
| Stretch | Distance | Speed | Time |
Three forms come up.
**What speed is needed for the rest?** "He must cover 120 km in 4 hours. He does the first 60 km at 20 km/h." That stretch took 3 hours. So 60 km remain and only 1 hour is left: he needs 60 km/h.

**Two speeds, total distance and total time given.** "400 km in 6 hours, partly at 80 km/h and partly at 60 km/h." Use the "pretend" idea you have met before. Pretend the whole 6 hours was at the slower speed: 360 km. The real distance is 40 km more. Each hour at the faster speed adds 20 km extra, so 2 hours were at 80 km/h, which is 160 km.

**Equal distances, total time given.** "Three equal distances at 3, 4 and 5 km/h take 47 minutes in all." Choose a convenient distance for each part, find the time that would take, and scale to the real time.

example.q: A man travels 300 km in 5 hours, partly at 50 km/h and partly at 70 km/h. What distance does he cover at 70 km/h?
steps: Pretend all 5 hours were at the slower speed: 50 x 5 = 250 km.
The real distance is 300 km, which is 50 km more.
Each hour at 70 km/h adds 70 - 50 = 20 km extra.
So the time at 70 km/h is 50 / 20 = 2.5 hours.
Distance at 70 km/h = 70 x 2.5 = 175 km.

check.q: A man has to cover 120 km in 4 hours. He covers the first 60 km at 20 km/h. At what speed must he cover the rest to arrive on time?
check.why: The first 60 km takes 3 hours. That leaves 60 km and 1 hour: 60 km/h. (30 km/h is the speed for the whole trip, which is no longer enough.)

lessons.title: Two people moving at once
lessons.plain: New: two moving people or vehicles. What matters is how fast the gap between them shrinks.
teach: When two things move at the same time, stop watching each one and **watch the gap between them**.
**Moving towards each other.** If A walks at 25 km/h and B at 35 km/h towards each other, every hour the gap shrinks by 25 + 35 = 60 km. So when they approach, **add the speeds**.
**One chasing the other.** If a policeman runs at 12 km/h after a thief running at 10 km/h, every hour the gap shrinks by only 12 - 10 = 2 km. So when they move the same way, **subtract the speeds**.
Either way:
**time to meet = gap between them / speed at which the gap shrinks**
The speed at which the gap changes is called the **relative speed**. It is not a new kind of speed; it is just how the two speeds combine.
Once you know **when** they meet, anything else follows from the first lesson. How far has A gone? A's speed x that time. How far has A still to go? The total minus that.
Two neat disguises:
- **On a circular track**, going opposite ways, they first meet when they have covered one full lap between them. The gap is the length of the track.
- **One reaches the end and turns back.** By the time they meet, the two together have covered **twice** the distance between the ends. Divide that by the sum of their speeds.
Keep the units the same here too. A gap of 500 metres with speeds in km/h should be written as 0.5 km.

example.q: Two cyclists are 90 km apart and ride towards each other at 12 km/h and 18 km/h. After how long do they meet?
steps: They are approaching, so add the speeds: the gap shrinks by 12 + 18 = 30 km every hour.
Time = gap / that speed = 90 / 30 = 3 hours.
Check: in 3 hours they ride 36 km and 54 km, which is 90 km together.

check.q: A is 200 metres behind B. A runs at 6 m/s and B runs at 4 m/s in the same direction. After how many seconds will A catch B?
check.why: Same direction, so subtract: the gap shrinks by 2 metres each second. 200 / 2 = 100 seconds. (20 seconds comes from adding the speeds, which is for approaching.)

lessons.title: When one starts earlier
lessons.plain: New: the two do not start together. Let the early one move alone first, then it is last lesson.
teach: "A train leaves A at 7 am. Another leaves B at 8 am towards it." The two-body method needs both to be moving. So deal with the lonely stretch first.
1. **Let the early starter travel alone** until the other one starts. Work out how far it goes.

2. **Find the gap at that moment.** If they are approaching, the gap is the distance between the towns **minus** what the early one has covered. If one is chasing the other, the gap **is** what the early one has covered: that is its lead.
3. **Now both are moving.** Time to meet = gap / speed at which it shrinks (add for approaching, subtract for chasing).
4. **Count that time from the later start**, and give the answer as a clock time or a distance, whichever is asked.
Step 4 is where marks are lost. If the second train left at 8 am and they meet 2 hours after that, the answer is 10 am, not 9 am.
If the question asks **how far from the start** the faster one overtakes, multiply the faster one's speed by the time it has been moving.

example.q: A leaves a town at 9 am at 30 km/h. B leaves the same town at 11 am at 50 km/h in the same direction. At what time does B overtake A?
steps: A travels alone from 9 to 11: 30 x 2 = 60 km. That is A's lead.
From 11 am both are moving the same way, so subtract: the gap shrinks by 50 - 30 = 20 km an hour.
Time to close 60 km = 60 / 20 = 3 hours.
Count from 11 am: B overtakes A at 2 pm.

check.q: Towns X and Y are 200 km apart. A train leaves X at 8 am towards Y at 40 km/h. Another leaves Y at 9 am towards X at 40 km/h. At what time do they meet?
check.why: By 9 am the first train has covered 40 km, so 160 km separate them. They approach at 80 km an hour: 2 hours. Counting from 9 am, they meet at 11 am.

lessons.title: Two last settings: stoppages, and what happens after they meet
lessons.plain: New: a bus that stops along the way, and two travellers who carry on after passing each other.
teach: Two smaller ideas to finish. They come up less often than the rest, and each is quick to learn.
**Stoppages.** "Without stops a bus averages 60 km/h. With stops it averages 48 km/h. How many minutes does it stop in each hour?"

Think about one hour of the journey. Without stopping the bus would cover 60 km. With stops it covers only 48 km, so it has **lost 12 km**. The time it stood still is the time it would have needed to drive those 12 km at its running speed: 12 / 60 of an hour, which is 12 minutes.
**minutes stopped per hour = (distance lost / running speed) x 60**
**After they meet.** "A and B start at the same time towards each other. After they meet, A takes 4 hours to reach the other end and B takes 9 hours. A's speed is 45 km/h; find B's."
There is a neat result for this exact situation. The two speeds are in the ratio of the **square roots of the two times, swapped over**:
**A's speed : B's speed = square root of B's time : square root of A's time**
Here that is the square root of 9 to the square root of 4, which is 3 : 2. A's 45 km/h is 3 parts, so B does 30 km/h.
The times in these questions are always chosen to be perfect squares (1, 4, 9, 16, 25), which is the clue that this result is wanted.

A related question gives two trains that each take the same number of hours for the journey but start at different times. That one is a head start in disguise (lesson 7): take each journey as a number of units, and let the early train go alone first.

example.q: Excluding stoppages the speed of a bus is 50 km/h, and including stoppages it is 40 km/h. For how many minutes does the bus stop per hour?
steps: In one hour without stops it would cover 50 km. With stops it covers 40 km.
It has lost 10 km.
At its running speed of 50 km/h, 10 km takes 10 / 50 of an hour.
That is 1/5 of an hour = 12 minutes.

check.q: Two cars start at the same time towards each other. After they meet, the first takes 1 hour to finish its journey and the second takes 4 hours. If the first car's speed is 60 km/h, what is the second car's speed?
check.why: Speeds are in the ratio of the square roots of the times, swapped: square root of 4 to square root of 1, which is 2 : 1. The first car's 60 km/h is 2 parts, so the second does 30 km/h.
